tur68-1: A neck collar does not help recovery. According to an NHS physiotherapy leaflet, research shows that a neck collar delays recovery.
tur68-2: Most people recover with simple advice and by staying active. In a large study in the United Kingdom of 599 people with ongoing symptoms, up to six physiotherapy sessions gave slightly faster recovery at 4 months than a single advice session; by 8 and 12 months there was no difference. If your symptoms are not settling, a personal assessment can help guide you. In a study in Australia of 172 people whose symptoms had lasted more than 3 months, a comprehensive 20-session physiotherapy exercise programme also did not reduce pain more than a single advice session with telephone support at 14 weeks, 6 months or 12 months.
tur68-3: These symptoms may point to the nerves in your neck being affected or to another serious problem; see a doctor or go to an emergency department without waiting. If your symptoms have not improved within a week, you can also see your doctor.
tur68-4: Woke up unable to turn your head, with your neck locked to one side? Wry neck is when a sudden spasm in the muscles on one side of the neck leaves the head tilted and turned to one side. It can be very painful and frightening, but it usually gets better on its own within a few days. Moving your neck slowly and regularly supports recovery; movement does not harm your neck.
tur68-5: No. Moving your neck slowly does not harm it; on the contrary, increasing movement day by day supports recovery. If the pain is very severe, you can rest for a day or so and then start moving slowly. The US physiotherapy guideline recommends, for recent-onset (acute) neck pain with limited movement, neck movement exercises and shoulder-blade and arm strengthening to help people stick with the programme.
tur68-7: Usually not; most mallet fingers do well with a splint alone. If a large piece of bone has come away with the tendon, surgery may be needed. This is usually a day-case procedure done under local anaesthetic, with the joint held by fine wires; the wires stay in for 3–4 weeks.
